surfaces.part: wooden frame border (top beam, side posts, corner caps)
dark stairwell opening with descending steps
step treads (light edge lines at rows 19 and 24, shadow at row 23)

answer.evidence: This is a flat floor stair-down: a wood frame (rows 3-29, about 29 px wide) around a dark pit (rows 8-18) with steps stepping down toward the viewer (rows 15-28). Treads at rows 20-22 and 25-28 are separated by light edge lines at rows 19 and 24 and a shadow at row 23. The whole piece is drawn as a plate seen from above. There is no vertical south face of 3 or more rows, and the bottom of the frame is only a 1-row dark outline at row 29. It reads as a flat top-down slab, which fits the flat kind.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is meant to be a 4x3-tile ground patch but reads as a single small framed stairwell, about 20px wide in source pixels. It has a tan/brown wooden frame, a dark interior and a grey step block, so it is an object rather than a ground surface and does not match the grass/paving references. The measured facts show 11 visible tones per tile, above the grass (3) and above the paving (7), with 0% near-flat coverage. Those numbers come from a tiny, high-contrast icon with only 13 colours in total, not from surface grain. The dark edge pixels are 100% neutral, so the interior and edge lines look like a near-black sticker outline. Only the wood frame shows any tint. The frame and steps have about 4 shading steps, against the references' 5-6 and their per-stone or per-tuft texture. There are no scallops, grain clusters or per-stone shading, and the form is a flat icon, not a tileable surface. A careful artist would not accept it as a ground patch next to the references.

answer.evidence: The silhouette is a near-square 29-30 px wide plate over rows 3-29. It is a wooden frame around a dark stairwell opening, seen from above. The frame is on all four sides, with matching corner pieces at the top and bottom. The steps inside are stacked horizontal bands (edge lines at rows 19 and 24, treads at rows 20-22 and 25-28) that descend into the dark, so they read as a floor decal rather than a standing volume. There is no south face below the plate: the bottom rows 26-29 are just the frame border, so the front face is under 3 rows. This matches a flat plate, which suits the 'flat' kind, but it is a top-down slab with no front elevation.

Inside the pit, light 1-row tread lines at rows 19 and 24 sit above 3-4 row risers, which suggests a descending staircase. That is consistent with the flat kind, so it is classed as a top-down slab with no front face.
